title: How @Cacheable decides whether to call your method
summary: Parse the annotations into operations, build a key from the arguments, look it up, and only invoke on a miss. The key generator is the part worth reading closely.
entry: Put a breakpoint in SimpleKeyGenerator.generateKey and call any @Cacheable method. Look at what it is given: the arguments, and nothing identifying the method.

steps.notice: What @EnableCaching imports. An advisor, an operation source and an interceptor - the same three pieces as transactions, which is not a coincidence.

Turns @Cacheable, @CachePut and @CacheEvict on a method into CacheOperation objects, once, and caches them. Note publicMethodsOnly defaults to true: a non-public @Cacheable method is not an error, it is simply never cached.
Four lines that delegate to the superclass. As usual, the class named after the feature is not where the work is.
The real logic: evict-before, look up, invoke on a miss, put, evict-after. condition is evaluated here before the lookup; unless is evaluated after the method has already run.

Nine lines, and the source of the worst caching bug you will meet. No arguments gives SimpleKey.EMPTY, one argument IS the key, several give a SimpleKey of them. The method is never part of the key, so two @Cacheable methods sharing a cache name and an argument type share entries.
The lookup. A cached null is a real hit, not a miss, because ConcurrentMapCacheManager allows null values by default.
